title: STAT+: We’re reading about BioNTech founders’ oncology startup, a long-acting GSK drug, and more
summary: The cofounders of BioNTech are in talks to raise about $1 billion for a new oncology company
text:
Hello again from STAT’s London outpost, with reporter Andrew Joseph here for Mr. Pharmalot. This newsletter will be off tomorrow and Friday, and while Thanksgiving is a U.S. holiday, it never hurts to take a moment to feel some gratitude, wherever you might be. In the meantime, a few tidbits for your day. …
The cofounders of BioNTech are in talks to raise about $1 billion for a new oncology company, as they prepare to step down from the Covid-19 vaccine maker, the Financial Times reports. Uğur Şahin and Özlem Türeci, the husband-and-wife team behind the German company, are speaking with potential investors about the funding round, which is being led by European venture capital firm Plural. Their new company will be called Arife and will focus on using messenger RNA to treat cancer.
A long-acting drug from GSK performed at least as well as an existing treatment for patients with eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, potentially setting up the medicine to be a less burdensome option for patients, Fierce Pharma shares. The non-inferiority study tested Exdensur, which was dosed just twice over a year, versus GSK’s other drug Nucala, which required monthly treatment. Exdensur resulted in remission rates at least on par with those from Nucala, and the drugs had similar adverse event rates. GSK says the results give it confidence that Exdensur now has a shot at becoming the first ultra-long-acting option for EGPA.

title: What to know before using AI agents for Black Friday shopping
summary: 59% of U.S. shoppers plan to use AI for holiday shopping this weekend, according to the National Retail Federation
text:
What to know before using AI agents for Black Friday shopping
Artificial intelligence is here to help with Black Friday.
This weekend, 59% of consumers plan on using AI to support their winter shopping, according to the National Retail Federation.
But AI has proven one way it is not unlike humans: It makes mistakes. The stakes of those hallucinations are much higher when your wallet – and holiday unwrapping memories – are on the line. These tools also become better shoppers when you hand over personal data, which also means giving up more information on your private life to massive tech companies.
Here are some tips – and notes of caution – before using AI as your personal holiday shopper.
Treat AI searches like a conversation with a kid
Traditional online shopping is about search terms and the infinite product scroll. AI is meant to be a conversation.
Unlike shopping on a retail website, AI platforms are designed to look more like texting apps. Prompt bars on these platforms sit on the bottom of the page, inviting a back and forth chat between user and bot about what to buy.
After all, it can be hard to know what keyword to plug in to shop for uncle before the Christmas exchange. AI instead allows for search based on a vibe – like describing that uncle's hobbies and personal style. If a shopper wants to buy a suitcase to support their uncle's European travel dreams, this makes it easier to narrow down the options.
"You can say if that bag is overstuffed, will it fit under the seat on JetBlue?" says Emily Pfeiffer, a principal analyst at Forrester who advises retailers and brands on digital commerce strategy, including for AI. "Don't give me the dimensions," she advises, "Tell me if it will suit my use case."
Pfeiffer cautions that even though AI is able to think through these nuanced shopping criteria, it works better with more hand holding.
"It's best if you imagine that it's a young child who will probably misinterpret your request," Pfeiffer said. "You want to be as specific and clear as possible."
AI Agents can shop for you. Be careful what you give them
Newer AI models can do more than talk and brainstorm. They can handle shopping tasks.
If shoppers are, for example, worried about holiday shipments arriving on time, AI can monitor an email inbox in order to track packages, even messaging a late shipper on the shopper's behalf. Beyond just suggesting a gift, agents can do the actual buying (with your money).
These are useful features, but require granting access to sensitive personal data, such as an inbox or credit card. One of the first questions Meta's AI agent platform Muse asks is if the user would like to connect their email and calendar.
Meta says its AI is highly secure. Everyone is assigned their own AI agent and the company promises that information shoppers share with it is kept private. Particularly sensitive information like credit card numbers, they say, are held separately and never viewed directly by the AI.

title: Poundland collapses putting 11,000 jobs at risk
summary: The discount chain has fallen into administration after its owners failed to find a buyer.
text:
Poundland collapses putting 11,000 jobs at risk
- Published
Poundland has collapsed into administration, putting 11,000 jobs at risk, after its owners failed to find a buyer to keep it in business.
The retailer's shops and distribution centres will remain open and continue to trade during the administration process with the business likely to be broken up and some of its stores sold off to rival retailers.
Poundland's US owners held talks with several bidders over a last-minute rescue deal, but no agreement was reached.
Poundland boss Barry Williams said in a note to staff that the board had "no alternative but to take this decision", but was making it with "sincere sadness and intense regret".
He said the US owners Gordon Brothers had removed "all borrowing facilities and access to our bank accounts" on 27 October, and adequate funds had not been released since then to keep the business solvent.
"Under these circumstances, it is impossible for the board of directors to see how Poundland can continue to operate as a going concern," he added.
'My income is gone'
Kelvin Blake, 62, who has worked for the firm for 25 years, and whose partner has been there 29 years, said he was feeling "down, depressed", and because of his age, feared he would not find a job elsewhere.
"We didn't want it, but it's come so now we've just got to face it and see what the future holds.
"My income's gone," he added. "Obviously, we'll be working until we're told to leave."
Alix Partners, which has been appointed as administrator, said they would look at all options for the business, "including sales of the business and its assets, either in whole or part".
"We appreciate this is a deeply concerning time for all involved - customers, suppliers and, in particular, Poundland colleagues," they said.
Gordon Brothers has been criticised over how it handled a potential sale of Poundland, with accusations the investment firm hoped to profit from selling off the chain's 600 shops and stock piecemeal after running it into the ground.
Gordon Brothers, which specialises in buying and restructuring distressed companies, has denied such claims.
On the funding question, Gordon Brothers said it had loaned the firm £85m over a year to help save it from insolvency.
But insiders critical of the US firm have said it stands to make its loans back and more from the insolvency process.
Previously, Gordon Brothers netted millions from liquidating the stock of fashion retailer LK Bennett, and in insolvency fees.
Labour MP Liam Byrne told the BBC the House of Commons' Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee will recall Gordon Brothers before Parliament.
He said: "I am really worried that a 'greed is good' approach to business by its owners has forced [Poundland] into an administration."
He added the committee wants to know "how much money they're ripping out and crucially, how do we make sure, as a country, that we don't have this kind of scenario unfold again".

title: RFK Jr. weighs in on plan to detonate toxic material in Iowa
summary: This morning, the Army plans to detonate a cache of “dangerously degraded” toxic material in Iowa, with experts warning of dangerous health consequences:
text:
Get your daily dose of health and medicine every weekday with STAT’s free newsletter Morning Rounds. Sign up here.
We aren’t sending a newsletter tomorrow, so a moment of sappiness today ahead of the holiday — I’ve been at STAT for 16 months, and I’m so thankful for the opportunities I’ve had to write and edit here. I learn something new just about every day (most recently that international graduate student enrollment has declined precipitously), and I’m lucky to have such wonderful, kind colleagues explaining the world of health and medicine.
If you, like me, are thankful for STAT’s coverage and hungry for more, we’ve got an amazing Cyber Week deal running. Pay $20 for six months of STAT+, and then $150 for the next year.
How does Kennedy spend his days? A new document dump offers a look
There were the hours spent prepping for Joe Rogan’s podcast, an afternoon filming videos at Kid Rock’s home in Nashville, and a meeting with the CEO of the company that makes Tylenol, just weeks before President Trump urged pregnant women not to take the drug because he claimed, without evidence, it was linked to autism.
These are some of the appointments documented in health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s calendar. In a show of “radical transparency,” HHS released the secretary’s partial calendar, which reflects his activities from Feb. 13, 2025, to June 19, 2026.
The calendar — part of a much broader release of documents from the Department of Health and Human Services — includes significant redactions and missing information. It shows, for example, only one meeting with one of his closest aides, Stefanie Spear. What else did our reporters find in this treasure trove of 92,000 documents? Read on.
Kennedy weighs in on plans to detonate toxic material in Iowa
This morning, the Army plans to detonate a cache of “dangerously degraded” toxic material in Iowa. Experts warn the planned explosion could send particles of lead into the air; an Army analysis found a plume could travel up to 100 miles, impacting homes and 350 farms.
The issue is attracting the attention of any number of federal agencies. The explosion’s after-effects are being tracked by the Environmental Protection Agency; FEMA is supporting possible evacuations. And Kennedy has weighed in several times from the perspective of HHS. Last week, former Iowa gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn posted on X that he had spoken with Kennedy about the planned detonation and that the secretary connected him with the White House to express his concerns. On Tuesday, Kennedy said on X that HHS is “working with state and local officials to assess potential lead exposure and support Iowa’s public health response,” adding that health department officials will “remain on the ground afterward to support the response and assist our partners with necessary cleanup.”

title: Buying new things feels wonderful. But it can also be a trap
summary: Constantly buying new things can be problematic, says journalist Eric Athas, author of the new book "Saying No to New." Here's how to break the cycle and find joy in what you already have.
text:
Buying new things feels wonderful. But it can also be a trap
Never miss a story or episode from Life Kit. Sign up for our weekly newsletter to get our journalism delivered directly to your inbox.
Buyer beware: Holiday shopping season is here. Is every sale calling your name? Is your virtual shopping cart overflowing?
Before you start buying everything, take note. There's a reason new things get us excited, says Eric Athas, author of Saying No to New: Why New Things Are Stealing Your Time, Money, and Happiness — and How to Take Back Your Life, published in September. Our brains are wired to seek out newness, and the retail industry is set up to keep us coming back for more as quickly as possible.
That constant consumption of novel possessions — whether they're brand-new, digital, secondhand or even free — can be problematic. "It's hard to be grateful for what you have if you're always on the lookout for something else," he says.
To break the cycle of chasing newness, we need to shop with more intention and find joy in what we already own, Athas says. In a conversation with Life Kit, he explains how. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
Why are we so drawn to seeking out new things?
Our brains are programmed to find new things interesting and old things boring.
If you think about our ancient ancestors, it was beneficial [for their survival] to explore new foods to eat and new territory and eventually explore different parts of the world.
There's also research that shows when we encounter something new, we get a little shot of dopamine. You get that feeling of excitement when you first use that new app or try that new video game or bring home a new gizmo for the kitchen.
What are some of the downsides of chasing newness?
New things can steal our happiness. Everyone can relate to the feeling of tearing open that new box or putting on that new outfit. You do feel joy and excitement from that initially.
But science says those feelings can't last. So we have to go out and get something else, and that's where we can get into this cycle of constantly chasing happiness in new things.
These days, it feels particularly hard to focus on what you have. There's so much pressure to buy new things. Why is that?
Everywhere we go, whether that's scrolling our favorite shopping app or browsing the aisle of our favorite store, there are little cues driving our [shopping] decisions. These companies have designs we don't even realize are engineering our choices.
For example, at the checkout page of a website or an app, there might be a countdown clock that says, "Save 25% if you make this purchase in three minutes." That's a tactic meant to whip up anxiety.
The other part of this is that you can buy new things faster than you've ever been able to before. It's all seamless and frictionless.
What can we do to create more friction between ourselves and the new things we want to buy?
Expand what I call "the new-thing gap." That's the time and distance bet

title: Sticker Shock Looms as a Major Challenge in Push for Single-Payer Healthcare
summary: Any discussion of a universal health plan in the U.S. always comes with concerns about massive costs. The challenge for proponents is to explain to voters that Americans already spend more than $5 trillion on healthcare each year.
text:
Sticker Shock Looms as a Major Challenge in Push for Single-Payer Healthcare
As an Oregon panel finalized its proposal for statewide universal healthcare this month, opposition had already coalesced around a familiar theme: The costs and the new taxes needed to support it will be staggeringly large. The panel’s estimates place the cost of the plan at $69.7 billion a year starting in 2032.
The same arguments are being made on the national level about “Medicare for All,” which gained renewed life after Democrats’ victorious blue wave in the midterms. One recent White House cost estimate pegged the annual price tag at $4.7 trillion.
But single-payer proponents, researchers, and academics are countering the perceived sticker shock with another stark reality: If you think universal healthcare would be expensive, you should see what we pay now.
“We already do spend trillions of dollars on healthcare,” said Cynthia Cox, a senior vice president at KFF, a health information nonprofit that includes KFF Health News. “It’s just that it’s not only spent by the federal government but also by states, individuals, private insurers, and other third-party payers.”
Increased government spending under a universal health plan would replace much, if not all, of what is currently being paid by companies and consumers, while extending health coverage to more people, its proponents argue. And they say many people would end up paying less for a universal health plan’s taxes than consumers now shell out in premiums and other out-of-pocket costs.
But those nuances represent some of the biggest challenges of selling a universal healthcare system to the public. Unless backers can figure out the messaging to alleviate fears of massive new taxes and government spending, current efforts to implement a single-payer, universal healthcare plan could be doomed to the same fate as previous efforts in places such as California, Massachusetts, and Vermont.
Educating the Public
In 2014, then-Vermont Gov. Peter Shumlin, a Democrat, pulled the plug on the state’s single-payer push. Difficulties in implementing the state’s healthcare exchange under the Affordable Care Act had sapped the political capital he needed to push through the plan’s tax increases, even though the state expected to save money for Vermonters overall.
Single-player ballot measures in California, Massachusetts, and Oregon also struggled to garner even a quarter of the voting public’s support.
The Democratic wave in this year’s midterm elections, however, ushered in a number of Medicare-for-All proponents, most notably Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, who campaigned on a universal healthcare platform. The change in congressional control is also expected to elevate Sen. Bernie Sanders, a Vermont independent who caucuses with Democrats and is the best-known advocate for Medicare for All, to chairman of the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.

title: Opinion: Washington and Beijing are building walls around biotechnology. That’s the wrong approach
summary: “Data show that the U.S.-China contest in biotechnology is not one race but several,” writes Michael S. Kinch.
text:
For more than a decade, my colleagues and I at the Center for Research Innovation in Biotechnology have tracked every experimental medicine that enters human testing anywhere in the world. Last December, I wrote in STAT that China had reached parity with the United States in terms of the absolute number of new drugs introduced into clinical trials each year. Starting in 2018, the rate of U.S. contributions began to stagnate. Meanwhile, in 2013, Chinese organizations had introduced about 30 new experimental drugs. A decade later, the number topped 400. And there is no reason to expect the momentum in either country is changing.
Over the past month, both governments have seemingly been moving to wall themselves off. On Oct. 16, Beijing proposed barring foreign acquisition of its companies’ proprietary cell and gene platforms. Within a week, the U.S. Department of the Treasury proposed restrictions that would bar Americans from taking equity stakes, forming joint ventures, or making limited-partner investments in Chinese biotech companies and their equipment suppliers.
The proposals from Beijing and Washington do not impact licensing. American drugmakers can keep licensing Chinese molecules, and Chinese companies may develop new medicines to sell to the U.S. and European companies.
That open door matters more than either wall. Data show that the U.S.-China contest in biotechnology is not one race but several. Restricting investment will not help America win the races it is already losing. The bigger threat to U.S. leadership is not Chinese capital. It is the erosion, at home, of the research enterprise that built America’s lead.
The Center for Research Innovation in Biotechnology’s newest analysis, published in September in Drug Discovery Today, emphasizes the importance of these continued engagements. My colleagues and I evaluated the 17,000 new drugs that first entered human trials between 2000 and 2024, separating them into eight different modalities. These ranged from conventional pills to gene therapies. The convergence in the numbers of overall active ingredients that we reported last year turned out to be anything but uniform when looking at the details.
The growth by China was concentrated in a key subset of biologics. By the late 2010s, Chinese sponsors often had introduced more, and more novel, cell therapies annually than American sponsors. By the early 2020s, China had matched or exceeded the U.S. in the introduction of new monoclonal antibodies, a commercially important class of biologic drugs. China took a commanding lead in certain categories of monoclonals, such as multispecific antibodies and drug conjugates.
The U.S. still holds a larger share in two categories: nucleic acid drugs and gene therapy. Dominance in both technologies reflects tools built over decades of Western public and private investment. Examples include lipid nanoparticles that conveyed SARS-CoV2 vaccines, viral vectors, and CRISPR gene editing.

title: In a time of rising costs, one Thanksgiving commodity is cheaper: cannabis
summary: Steep discounts for "Green Wednesday," one of the highest-selling days for cannabis, help customers keep costs down. But experts say retailers are feeling the pinch.
text:
In a time of rising costs, one Thanksgiving commodity is cheaper: cannabis
This Thanksgiving season, Americans are paying more for almost everything: travel costs have soared, and the price of food has risen. Bringing wine to the family dinner? That costs more, too.
But there's one thing consumers buy at high rates that will actually get cheaper this time of year: marijuana.
Known in the industry as "Green Week" or "Green Wednesday," the days ahead of Thanksgiving have come to rival famed stoner holiday 4/20 as the day cannabis dispensaries see the most sales — and highest foot traffic — of the year.
In most dispensaries around the country, that means steep discounts, doorbuster specials and exclusive products. It's a good deal for customers, who line up in long queues as they await their turn with the so-called budtenders behind the counter.
Cannabis in the U.S. is a $30 billion industry with legal marketplaces in 24 states and the nation's capital, according to Whitney Economics, a firm that specializes in economic research and consulting on the business of cannabis. But in recent years, the deep discounts that have drawn in customers — and kept them coming back for weeks like this one — have squeezed retailers and resulted in a revenue decline in the legal market.
As the week began at The Forest, a dispensary in Baltimore, shoppers were stocking up for the holiday week.
A pack of gummies to bring to Friendsgiving in lieu of alcohol. A sparkling THC-infused beverage for those canna-curious in-laws. Or a holiday staple: some pre-rolls to share on an evening walk.
On bright screens posted around the store, discount offers flashed: 25% off edibles, read one; 30% off for medical patients, read another. An extra $5 off for bringing in cans of food for the store's holiday drive.
Kelley Vinton, 36, is a regular at The Forest. She's a medical marijuana user and usually sticks to a strict weekly budget, she said. But on Monday, she threw in a few little extras — for the "cousin walk," Vinton said.
"You know, you take a little breaky-poo with your cousins, and we live in the country, so we just walk, usually before dinner," Vinton said. "We smoke a joint, and we get nice and high, and get some munchies and get ready for dinner."
The federal government still classifies recreational marijuana as a Schedule I drug, meaning it is considered to have "high potential for abuse," according to the Drug Enforcement Administration. But medical cannabis was reclassified this year to Schedule III, a category shared by drugs like Tylenol with codeine and anabolic steroids.
In 2025, Whitney Economics found, revenue was down across the industry thanks to an oversupply of plant product and declining prices, driven by the discount culture of cannabis retailers.
It was the first year since 2014 — when Colorado and Washington became the first states to legalize cannabis sales for recreational use — that the industry saw a dip, according to an analysis by Whitney Economics.

title: Medicare Open Enrollment: Here’s What’s Changing, and What Mistakes To Avoid
summary: Medicare’s zero-premium drug plans are disappearing, millions are losing their plans, and the average prescription drug plan premium could rise 50% if you stay put. Here’s what to check.
text:
Medicare Open Enrollment: Here’s What’s Changing, and What Mistakes To Avoid
Annual open enrollment is underway for Medicare, the federal program that provides health insurance to roughly 70 million people. The coverage choices are complex and often consequential.
Medicare provides health insurance to people 65 or older, as well as to some younger people with disabilities or certain health conditions. But it isn’t one plan. It’s more like a build-your-own-insurance menu.
Roughly half of beneficiaries are enrolled in traditional Medicare, which consists of Parts A and B. Administered by the federal government, the plan covers hospital stays, skilled nursing care, doctor visits, outpatient care, and preventive screenings. Enrollees can typically see any healthcare provider who accepts Medicare, and they rarely need approval for diagnostic tests, such as MRIs and CT scans. However, there’s no cap on out-of-pocket expenses in traditional Medicare, and it doesn’t cover most prescriptions or dental, vision, or hearing services.
As a result, most traditional Medicare enrollees buy extra coverage from private insurance companies under Medicare Part D, the prescription drug plan. Some also buy a Medigap policy that covers the costs traditional Medicare leaves behind, such as deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance.
This year, the other half of Medicare beneficiaries opted for privately offered, all-in-one managed-care plans known as Medicare Advantage, usually including prescription drug coverage, dental, and vision. The drawbacks are smaller networks and a greater likelihood that treatments and medications will require prior authorization. Like beneficiaries in traditional Medicare, Medicare Advantage participants also pay Part B premiums.
“People really need to do their research before they enroll in Medicare, because there are trade-offs,” said David Lipschutz, a co-director at the Center for Medicare Advocacy.
The Hassle Saves Money
Every fall, insurers that offer Part D and Advantage plans send enrollees a critical document known as an Annual Notice of Change. It’s a cheat sheet outlining what will be different in the following year: premiums, deductibles, covered drugs. Consumer advocates and Medicare experts say people sometimes make the costly mistake of throwing it out or filing it away without reading it. Can’t find it? Call the insurer and ask for another copy.
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services projects that the average Part D premium will increase less than $1 a month for a standalone prescription drug plan, describing the market as stable. But that average doesn’t tell the whole story. An analysis by KFF, the health policy research nonprofit that includes KFF Health News, found that enrollees who stay in their prescription drug plan will see a 50% increase on average, from $34 to $51. About 10.4 million people could pay higher premiums, not including higher deductibles and coinsurance costs.

title: US stocks fall further as fears over AI intensify
summary: All three main US indexes were down in early trading, with the tech-dominated Nasdaq down almost 4%.
text:
US stocks fall further as fears over AI intensify
- Published
Big technology firms connected to AI continued to see share prices fall on Wednesday, with stock in Nvidia and Anthropic dropping sharply in early trading.
The surge in Nvidia shares after boss Jensen Huang was reinstated was temporary, and the general stock sell-off continued, with all three main US stock market indices down. The tech-dominated Nasdaq has shed over 2%.
The declines come amid concerns over the level and sustainability of AI investment which has rattled investors in recent weeks.
Shares in other major tech firms, including Amazon, Tesla and SpaceX, Micrsoft and Meta were also down.
Nvidia's share price was down 8% in early trading on Wednesday, extending Tuesday's slide as the boost from Huang's return eased.
The resignation and subsequent reinstatement of Nvidia boss Jensen Huang after revelations of his extra marital affairs has seen the market value of the world's premier AI chipmaker fluctuate wildly.
Given Nvidia's position as both supplier and financier of many other firms involved in the AI rollout, its rocky fortnight has had a wider impact.
The US government also announced a raft of new tariffs on countries and trading partners on Wednesday as part of President Donald Trump's flagship trade policy.
The value of big tech companies have sheltered the US economy from global economic shocks, including tariffs, but share prices in recent weeks have been volatile in response to the US midterm elections and other events in the AI industry.
- Faisal Islam: Fears over the AI boom haven't gone away 
  - Published1 day ago
Investors have taken fright at Democrat gains in the US midterm elections, with many having campaigned for tougher regulation of AI firms and even a moratorium on the development of new data centres.
Questions also remain about whether the huge sums being invested in AI will eventually pay off.
"It seems that these companies are trying to one-up each other on the amount of money that they're spending but you have to show that it's worth it, and that's where Wall Street is saying I don't know," said Todd Schoenberger, chief investment officer at CrossCheck Management.
Despite concerns, investment in AI is expected to exceed $1 trillion in 2026, according to investment bank Goldman Sachs, which said the technology will remain the "dominant driver of business investment growth" next year.
Shares in Anthropic continued to trade below the $83 they debuted at last week, while Amazon shares fell by more than 5%.
The declines come ahead of the US stock market closing for Thanksgiving on Thursday before opening for a shortened session on Friday.

title: Despite stalling in court, Trump restrictions on foreign students have had a chilling effect on enrollment
summary: New data show a clear drop in the enrollment of international graduate students, a key piece of the U.S. biomedical workforce.
text:
Even as judges have blocked visa restrictions and other limits on foreign scholars and scientists, the Trump administration is winning outside court. New data show a clear drop in the enrollment of international graduate students, a key piece of the U.S. biomedical workforce.
That paradox was on full display last week. On Nov. 16, a federal judge issued a final ruling blocking a proposed four-year cap on how long international students and postdoctoral researchers can remain in the country. The next day, a judge in a separate case issued a preliminary injunction preventing the administration from narrowing eligibility for a work authorization program widely used by foreign students.
To student advocates like Fanta Aw, CEO of the nonprofit NAFSA: Association of International Educators, the rulings represented two wins in two days. “I’ve always believed that our judicial systems are strong and are very much still in play, and I felt relieved,” said Aw, whose organization is a plaintiff in both cases. “Our members, and in particular our students, I felt, were vindicated.”
But data released the same day as the ruling in the visa time limit case paint a less celebratory picture. A survey of more than 800 U.S. institutions conducted by the Institute of International Education found that foreign student enrollment for the current academic year has decreased 9% overall compared with 2025, with a 15% drop among newly enrolled students and graduate students. While IIE won’t have complete data until next year, the preliminary numbers suggest this will be the third consecutive year graduate enrollment has dropped — with the largest year-to-year decrease in at least 20 years, according to historical data from the nonprofit.
That trend extends to biomedicine, where foreign students make up nearly a quarter of life science Ph.D. graduates, according to new survey data from the Association of American Medical Colleges. A poll of 37 AAMC member institutions showed that the number of international students starting biomedical Ph.D. programs has decreased by about 30% since 2024, more than twice the 14% overall decline in matriculation in these programs.
The growing body of data as well as STAT’s interviews with students and immigration experts suggest that, despite the legal losses, the Trump administration’s policies on immigration have had a chilling effect on students considering coming to the U.S., and on those who are already here. Meanwhile, enrollment of foreign students is rising at some Asian universities, and experts warn that these opposing trends could jeopardize the nation’s biomedical preeminence and that it could take years to repair the loss of trust from students who no longer see the U.S. as a welcoming destination.
“People are looking at us from overseas, going, ‘We don’t really recognize this country,’” said Elizabeth Goss, an immigration attorney based in Boston. Even if Democrats’ new majority in Congress prevents further restrictions, she ad

title: Nvidia's board under fire for handling of CEO's alleged affairs
summary: Even as Jensen Huang has returned to work, Nvidia's board is facing criticism over how it handled the crisis brought on by the CEO's alleged affairs.
text:
Nvidia's board under fire for handling of CEO's alleged affairs
Even as Jensen Huang has returned to work, Nvidia's board is facing criticism over how it handled the crisis brought on by the CEO's alleged affairs.
MICHEL MARTIN, HOST:
How did a board that unanimously decided that its CEO must go decide a few days later to bring him right back? We're talking about Nvidia and its founder, former and now current CEO Jensen Huang. NPR's Andrea Hsu has been gathering reaction to the board's handling of the crisis, and she's with us now to tell us more.
Good morning, Andrea.
ANDREA HSU, BYLINE: Good morning.
MARTIN: OK, so let me just point out here that at an all-hands meeting on Tuesday, Huang apologized for hurting his family and violating the company's code of conduct. That's according to a livestream of the meeting which was viewed by The New York Times. He also reportedly said that President Trump didn't pressure the board into bringing him back. NPR has reached out to Nvidia for confirmation of this, but hasn't heard back. You've been hearing from people who know how boards are meant to operate. What are you hearing from them?
HSU: Yeah. Well, there's been criticism from both those who think Jensen Huang shouldn't have been brought back and also those who think it was the right thing to do. And, Michel, let's remember the role of boards - they exist to make informed and deliberate decisions that are in the best interests of the company and its shareholders. In many instances, they are the only mechanism of accountability for companies and CEOs. And in the case of Nvidia, you know, a lot of people say the board fell short on these duties, and we've asked Nvidia for a response to that, but we haven't heard back on that, either.
MARTIN: Now, recognizing that you're getting a range of opinions there, do these experts have thoughts on what should have happened?
HSU: Yeah. Well, many are saying that the board should have made different choices. Our colleague Shannon Bond spoke with Rob Lalka. He's a professor at Tulane's Freeman School of Business (ph), and he points out that in the last decade, there have been a number of high-profile cases similar to what allegedly happened at Nvidia - you know, a CEO having an affair with an employee. It happened at Intel, McDonald's, Nestle. And Lalka says those boards followed their policies, and those CEOs were out. They decided it had to happen to preserve company values and credibility. But then, as for Nvidia, here's what Lalka says.
ROB LALKA: The board basically went around its entire process that it had set in place for that investigation to put him back into power.
MARTIN: But you also mentioned that there are people who think bringing Huang back was the right thing to do. Say more about that.

title: It’s the Paperwork, Not the Work, Causing Enrollees To Lose Medicaid in Nebraska
summary: Data from the months after the state’s early rollout of new federal work requirements bolsters concerns that red tape will leave many stuck without coverage.
text:
It’s the Paperwork, Not the Work, Causing Enrollees To Lose Medicaid in Nebraska
The state’s early rollout of federal work requirements offers a potential preview of the challenges ahead in the rest of the country.
When Nebraska chose to implement Medicaid work requirements eight months before it was called for under President Donald Trump’s sweeping 2025 budget law, many health policy analysts panned the decision. They worried people would lose coverage because of system glitches.
Many also watched the Cornhusker State’s experience to see whether it would offer lessons to the more than three dozen other states that would follow it in 2027.
On Nov. 13, the Trump administration gave states the option of taking extra time to get ready.
They’ll have until July 2027, rather than January, to begin dropping coverage for people who don’t meet the work requirements. States have until Dec. 11 to decide whether they will still fully implement the requirements on Jan. 1 and begin dropping those who don’t comply or start refusing new coverage to people who aren’t working.
Congressional Democrats, who often criticized Medicaid work requirements on the campaign trail and have sided with states in urging a reprieve from the January deadline, claimed victory.
“The Trump-Vance Administration finally admitted what Democrats have said from the very beginning: Republicans’ chaotic maze of red tape requirements jeopardize the health care of millions of Americans,” Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) and Rep. Frank Pallone (D-N.J.) said in a statement.
Democrats’ massive election victories in November will give them control of both chambers of Congress next year. Top Democrats said they’ll prioritize legislation to stop the Medicaid work requirements before they’re fully enforced.
The Basics
Not everyone in Medicaid must comply with the new requirements. They will apply only to low-income adults who were made eligible for the program in 43 states, along with Washington, D.C., that chose to expand Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act or through a special waiver from the federal government. Most enrollees are already working, surveys show, so to comply, they will only have to provide proof of their employment to their states.
But that may not be as simple as it sounds, depending on how well states notify Medicaid beneficiaries of the requirement and how easy they make it to submit paperwork. The Congressional Budget Office estimated the new rules would increase the number of uninsured U.S. adults by 5.3 million by 2034.
The rules require work, volunteering, or school attendance for at least 80 hours a month. There are several exemptions, including for people who care for young children or those with disabling medical conditions, a category called “medically frail.”
It all adds up to about 20 million people subject to work Medicaid requirements, including about 70,000 in Nebraska.

title: Energy price increase 'could put me in hospital'
summary: People on Teesside share their views on the news energy bills are expected to increase by 26%.
text:
Energy price increase 'could put me in hospital'
- Published
A hike in energy costs in the new year has prompted concerns many families will see a hard winter.
Energy bills are expected to increase by 26% from January after a surge in gas prices sparked by the Iran war, with the government saying it will pay millions of households £100 from 4 January to help cover winter costs on top of an existing VAT cut on electricity.
However, residents in Stockton-on-Tees and Darlington said that was not enough to mitigate the rise of about £440 annually.
Kathleen Simms, from Stockton, said: "If I can't have the heating on, I'm going to end up in hospital."
Simms, who is in remission from cancer and has a lung condition, said: "It's hard to live now, if they put the bills any higher, we don't know what we can live on.
"We rely on food banks and stuff which we don't really like doing, but if it comes to that crunch, we have to."
In Darlington town centre, Alice Smith Burns said she was fortunate she could "suck up" the extra charges as she lived with her parents, but knew that option was not available to everyone.
"I have my daughter with me, and I'd rather she's not just sat there with blanket on her," Smith Burns said. "I'd rather she just had that heat source.
"I think especially as a young parent, if there are other young parents out there, it might be harder for those kinds of people.
"For low income households, it's a massive toll on everyone."
Alexandra Blowers said she was fortunate to have solar panels on her home as they had brought her electricity bills down.
However, she still predicts she will limit her heating use.
"The gas price is obviously not the cheapest right now," she said.
"We do tend to not put the heading on as much as we might like to, I layer up because I do tend to get quite cold."
Tim Robinson said he also felt fortunate as he would not be hit by the 26% rise immediately due to being on a fixed rate.
However, he said he did not know how others would cope.
"I think the vulnerable always have to be protected no matter what circumstance they're in, whether it's in relation to heating, energy or food," he said.
"If you don't look after the vulnerable in society, then you're a very poor society."
Staff at Stockton Citizens' Advice said they expected to see a wave of people already in debt accessing services in the coming months.
"We know our clients are struggling enough as it is anyway," said CEO Sarah McPhie.
"We know that in the Tees Valley, 70% of those children who are growing up in poverty are coming from a working household and unfortunately those working households are not going to see the increase in their wages compared to the increase in their energy prices."

title: STAT+: RFK Jr. spills his calendar into public, but leaves much to the imagination
summary: A partially redacted calendar showing health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s activities was made public on Tuesday.
text:
WASHINGTON — A new website launched by the Trump administration provides centralized access to more than 92,000 public records from the Department of Health and Human Services and the agencies it oversees — including partially redacted entries from health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s calendar.
While many of the records were previously available, the health department heralded the launch of the site as a sign of its “radical transparency.”
In June, after a New York Times report referred to him as disengaged with the job, Kennedy said on social media that his calendar was publicly available, though no such calendar had been made available for the media or the public before Tuesday. A number of Freedom of Information Act requests filed by STAT reporters had previously gone unanswered and even unacknowledged and do not appear to be included in the Tuesday release.
Much of the secretary’s partial calendar, which reflects his activities from Feb. 13, 2025, to June 19, 2026, is redacted, including some private calls taken by the secretary. One of his closest aides at the agency, Stefanie Spear, appears to be listed only once in the calendar. References to other notable meetings are not redacted, including one that would ultimately lead to the ouster of a short-lived director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Susan Monarez.

title: As States Lose OB-GYNs, Some Look To Limit Medical Malpractice Risk
summary: Since 2025, at least four states have enacted laws restricting medical malpractice lawsuits. Patient advocates warn that the laws impose more of a burden on families harmed during childbirth and often pass with little attention.
text:
As States Lose OB-GYNs, Some Look To Limit Medical Malpractice Risk
When Anyssa Zancanella’s water broke during a family vacation near Salt Lake City, she expected better care there than she could get back home in rural Rock Springs, Wyoming, where many patients are flown out for emergency treatment.
Instead, a crisis unfolded. Staff kept raising her doses of Pitocin, a drug that strengthens contractions, while the fetal monitor recorded mounting distress: The baby wasn’t getting enough oxygen. It took nearly 12 hours for the then-19-year-old to get an emergency cesarean section after the monitor showed signs of fetal distress, according to court records.
Azaylee, now 7, was born with brain damage, likely from a reduced supply of oxygen and blood flow during delivery, causing cognitive disabilities, according to her family’s complaint. Last year, a judge found Steward Health Care, a Dallas-based for-profit health system that owned the West Valley City, Utah, hospital at the time, liable for gross medical negligence — and awarded the family $951 million. Steward Health Care did not respond to a request for comment for this article.
Medical malpractice lawsuits against OB-GYNs are common in the U.S. healthcare system — childbirth can carry high risk and serious consequences. As a result, medical malpractice insurance costs for OB-GYNs are higher than for other specialties. Hospital administrators repeatedly cite the costs of those lawsuits and medical liability premiums as a reason to close their labor and delivery units. So, in recent years, state lawmakers began turning to what they say is a solution: tougher limits on malpractice lawsuits.
Since 2025, at least four states, including Oklahoma, have enacted restrictions on medical malpractice suits. Utah added protections shielding physicians’ personal assets. New Mexico capped punitive damages, which punish wrongdoing beyond financial losses, and raised the standard of proof, requiring “clear and convincing” evidence for punitive damages. And Arkansas shortened the window a patient can file those suits after delivery.
The laws often pass with little fanfare, and patient advocates warn they impose more of a burden on families harmed during childbirth, many of whom don’t realize for years that they’ve been survivors of medical malpractice.
“You really don’t know what you need to be looking for. You just know that you’re hurting,” said Deirdre Dickson-Gilbert, founder and national director of the National Medical Malpractice Advocacy Association. “And by the time you find out, the statutes of limitation are over with.”
Other critics say the actions ignore alternative ways to retain obstetricians, such as addressing abortion bans, which several states pursued in this month’s midterm elections.

title: What's gone wrong at Poundland?
summary: Poundland has collapse into administration. Why?
text:
What's gone wrong at Poundland?
- Published
The future of Poundland hangs in the balance after the discount retailer's collapse into administration.
Its owner, US investment firm Gordon Brothers, put it up for sale in September, but then rejected offers to keep the business afloat.
Poundland has a major presence on the High Street, with 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, where it trades under the Dealz brand.
Its collapse puts the jobs of its 11,000 employees at risk, as well as potentially thousands of others at firms that supply the retailer.
How have we got here?
Have people stopped shopping at Poundland?
People have not stopped shopping at Poundland - quite the opposite.
Although the chain was struggling when it was sold by Pepco last year for £1, the business turned a corner over the year to September, going from a £68m loss to an £18.1m profit before interest, tax and certain accounting charges.
Going into the vital Christmas period, first-quarter like-for-like sales were up 7% and operational profits of £1.9m were up £1.2m on last year.
According to Julie Palmer, managing partner at insolvency specialist Begbies Traynor, "this isn't a story about shoppers abandoning Poundland".
She told the BBC the tills were "busier than they were a year ago", adding that on the face of it a turnaround seemed "well under way".
However, Gordon Brothers had been restricting Poundland's access to cash needed to restock stores and meet day-to-day expenses.
So why is it now in administration?
Poundland faced "a funding and ownership problem rather than a trading collapse", according to Palmer.
However, while Poundland boss Barry Williams claimed the business was making a "strong recovery", Gordon Brothers painted a different picture, saying the chain remained "challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading".
It said it had provided significant funding to support the company's ability to trade since it acquired the business.
- Poundland collapses putting 11,000 jobs at risk 
  - Published2 hours ago
- Poundland workers 'in limbo' over firm's future 
  - Published1 day ago
It has also made about £18m from a combination of debt interest payments and other fees and charges.
As well as being Poundland's owner, it is one of its lenders, and is owed loans, including a £22.5m shareholder loan it inherited when it bought the business for £1.
As the main creditor, Gordon Brothers would be first in line to get paid back if the business goes under - but its suppliers are not.
"When the owner is also the main lender, its first priority is recovering [loans]," says Palmer. "Sometimes the route that best protects the lender is different from the one that saves the most jobs, and that tension is why this has become such a political story."

title: What should it cost to insure a home in wildfire country?
summary: Some California homeowners have spent thousands making their homes safer from wildfires. Yet all that work has barely made a dent in their insurance bills. Should they be getting a bigger break?
text:
What should it cost to insure a home in wildfire country?
As a homeowner in rural Northern California, I've lost a lot of sleep worrying about fires. It's not just that big, destructive ones are becoming more common. It's that finding affordable and reliable home insurance has become a nightmare. Without it, the most valuable asset I own could literally go up in smoke. And we've been stuck in a broken insurance market, hoping someone or something can fix it.
Which is why I was so gripped by Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi's recent two-part series on our Planet Money podcast. And it's left me thinking about the economics of making our communities safer. Insurers are spending money to figure out how to keep houses from burning down. Yet some California homeowners tell him they're investing heavily to make their homes and communities safer, and all that work has barely made a dent in their insurance bills.
In the first episode, Alexi goes to a destruction lab in South Carolina where researchers use "crash-test dummies for houses" — the type of wonderful turn of phrase that we love Alexi for — to figure out what actually works to help homes survive climate disasters. They literally light mock houses on fire and subject them to hail and hurricane-force winds to see what happens to them.
Who pays for this lab? Some of the world's biggest insurance companies. They want to know how risky homes are to insure and which building designs will limit damage and shrink the payouts they have to make if disasters strike. It's a pretty wild way to tackle an increasingly urgent question: can we make homes that can better withstand fires and other disasters?
Alexi touches on this in the pod, but insurers have been running experiments like these for more than a century. Back in the early 20th century, scientists at an insurer-funded organization called Underwriters Laboratories tested out new kinds of electrical wiring and consumer appliances to try to reduce the risk of costly fires and electrical accidents. An outfit called the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety does something similar for cars, using crash tests to push for safer auto designs.
Fighting moral hazard in fire country
The insurance industry is way more interesting than most people give it credit for. Part of the magic is obvious. It can insulate us from financial devastation. But there can also be magic in how insurers figure out how big risks really are and what it takes to reduce them. That destruction lab in South Carolina is an amazing example of that.
But Alexi's reporting has me wondering whether insurers could do more to reduce risk. It has to do with this weird thing about insurance. If someone else picks up the tab when something goes wrong, you may have less reason to do everything you can to make sure that it doesn't go wrong in the first place. Economists call this "moral hazard." It's the idea that insurance can reduce incentives to mitigate risk.
